article.plain_text:
Superintelligence is arriving. How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.
As someone who has spent much of my life in math and science, I see the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as clearly marking the beginning of a significant change. For most who have studied math, this represents the absolute pinnacle of intellectual accomplishment—nothing humanity has ever accomplished compares to proving the Riemann Hypothesis in terms of sheer intellectual might and strength. As someone who grew up in Los Alamos, New Mexico, many physicists would agree that the discovery of the atomic bomb is a homework problem compared to the Riemann Hypothesis. It is hard to overstate the magnitude of discovery that we have just witnessed—completed with the help of an alien mind that we don’t understand.
For those who did math competitions, there was a similar moment of “oh shit everything is about to change” when the models began acing the AIME in December 2024 with o3. The hardest AIME problems are much harder in terms of sheer intellectual difficulty than the problems that even the most advanced engineers and business people need to solve on a day-to-day basis. There of course is domain-specific knowledge, context, know-how, and other tactical constraints that were needed to unlock the models across other areas, but lack of raw intelligence was not the bottleneck. And in fact, the progress across other domains over the past 2 years as we’ve mitigated these non-intelligence factors has been immense—we have seen coding be nearly solved, the emergence of extremely powerful cyber capabilities, and strong agentic capabilities which have enabled the models to become general-purpose useful aides.
Again the key insight here was simply that the hardest AIME problems are intellectually very difficult, far more difficult than most coding work, most cyber work, most business work, etc., and over the past two years we have been filling in the gaps to enable the models to accomplish those things.
To be clear, AIME is an extracurricular activity for teenagers; the Riemann Hypothesis may be the most intellectually demanding problem humanity has ever devised, which some of the most brilliant humans over the past 150 years have dedicated their lives to. At MIT, my professors would have said the hardest intellectual problems in nearly every major field of human study are “easier” than the Riemann Hypothesis, albeit with other challenges such as experimentation, data, and feedback loops. The remaining gaps for models to greatly surpass humanity in every field are no longer intelligence; they are domain-specific know-how, plumbing, and experimentation. This means it is likely that AI will become the greatest contributor of progress across nearly every field, vastly outperforming the best humans.
Notably, this is likely true of AI research. Most researchers would agree that AI research is certainly much less intellectually demanding than solving the Riemann Hypothesis. The models are clearly going to be intelligent enough to automate all of AI research and be clearly superhuman at improving themselves—along with massively accelerating biological research, weapons research, economics research, and more. The implications are enormous. In the same way that the math community has not fully digested the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, nearly every field could be accelerated at a pace beyond what humans can understand or monitor.
It is now incredibly important for us to be thoughtful about the future we want and how we get there. It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement. It is equally hard to imagine a world where humanity maintains control with superintelligence that is 1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field. Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.
I notice a particular form of lazy thinking within the AI industry, which is that ASI is inevitable and the only problem to solve is how to do it safely, but there is much more at stake. We should not be okay with a “handover” of society to AI. We should endeavor ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment. I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.

full_text:
i forgot about this until @ScottWu46 reminded me, but back in january 2017 when we were 19, scott and i had lunch in SF

at lunch, we talked about how our IMO/IOI/math competition gang could be the next paypal mafia. i knew the competition kids were geniuses by any standard, and felt confident in time we could take the tech world by storm

fast forward nearly 10 years later, and many of our friends from that time are some of the most exciting people in AI and technology (@ScottWu46, @akshat_b, @chameleon_jeff, Jerry Ma, @randomjohnnyh, @0xShitTrader, @stevenkplus1, @thejessezhang, @vickie_ye_, @alexwei_, @demi_guo_, @d_m_ziegler, @hughbzhang, @_mohansolo, @MarkSellke, and many others i'm sure i'm forgetting)

i'm now at that age where i reminisce about everyone i grew up with, and i've known most of these people since middle school (via MATHCOUNTS!). even though we were scattered around the country, we would gchat about math problems and hang out on AoPS, then we did math/algo camps together, and then we did internships together.

very crazy to think about the degree of sheer brilliance of this group when we were just teenagers, and so special to see so many go on to leave their mark on the world.

note to parents: if your kid is on gchat all day solving math problems with some anonymous group of cross-country asian kids, (s)he may just turn out alright.

full_text:
wildwood is a true marvel of human artistry, craftsmanship, and storytelling. i honestly found it even better than You Can See Everything (gasp!).

[spoilers if you read on]

an interesting trend in both wildwood and hoppers is how they handle death. they’re both movies for young people that treat death as inevitable and natural, and both expose the audience to a surprising amount of it. this feels quite different from the cleaner moral universes of much of modern disney and pixar.

both movies also have strong themes of non-intervention. of course, this is environmentally motivated, but there’s a broader Buddhist / Taoist morality running through both films: the world has a natural balance, and our attempts to impose our own ideas of goodness upon it can be destructive.

this feels quite different from the more Christian-inflected morality of overcoming evil. in these films, nature isn’t inherently good or evil, and trying to eliminate everything we perceive as bad can itself be the source of harm.

i wonder if this reflects a broader generational shift toward stories where it’s increasingly difficult to know what’s “right” or “wrong”, and where good intentions aren’t enough to make an action good.

both films feel like spiritual siblings to princess mononoke, questioning the hubris of humans who believe they can impose their will on the natural world.

wildwood is also visually spectacular and a complete and utter artistic achievement. it is always so rewarding to see fresh new takes on what a movie can be and how stories can be told.

huge fan, go see it!

REMY OR LINGUINI?

for those of you who have seen ratatouille, one of the great questions in the ai age: are we remy or linguini?

are the humans in control of the combined entity (we are remy), or are the ai in control and we are simply the meat proxies (we are linguini)?

muse is our partner to help make that happen. ultimately, we are pulling the hairs (?), and it is our vision that ends up on the plate (?), but over time we will accomplish things that we could not do without muse.

(obviously this metaphor is super confusing because i'm saying the humans are the rat, but if you watched the movie you catch my drift)

we launched muse a month ago today

for the past month, reality felt like a dream. we watched the world catch fire with muse. every day we read stories of people saving money and precious time. every day it made people’s lives better in small and big ways. every day i watched the muse team pour their hearts into bringing a little more wonder in the world.

the response to muse has surpassed anything i could have imagined. i know the muse team will remember it for the rest of our lives.

it is easy to become jaded in tech. products launch every day but they very rarely make any dent in the world. but i have seen muse make a real difference for moms, for grandpas, for students, for coworkers. many of you using it in ways we never expected. 

thank you to the muse team. thank you to everyone who’s tried muse. this is only the beginning. we have so much more to build.

article.plain_text:
Most people never say what they want. It’s not because we don’t want. We want fiercely and constantly. It happens in the moments before falling asleep or while daydreaming on the car ride home. We want to spend more time with our families, overcome social anxiety, eat healthier food, open a bakery, build an app, or just find a few more moments of calm in a hectic life. But rarely do we get to even express these dreams, and even more rarely do they ever come true.
When we can’t name our dreams, we mostly can’t reach them. The world is a maze of forms and gatekeepers and schedules and obstacles, and most dreams die by a thousand paper cuts long before they are said aloud. They die in the not-knowing-where-to-start and in the phone calls never made. 
Every unrealized want is a quiet tragedy of human potential.
Now imagine every person on earth with a second mind beyond their own. A general manager whose whole job is to find out what you want and make sure it happens. Someone that hears the half-sentence, “I feel like there’s something more I could be doing,” and helps fill in the blanks. This might not be a genie in a bottle, but it can be someone that says, “This is the thing you’ve been dreaming of your whole life. Let’s go get it. Here’s how.” And then builds a plan. Sends the email. Makes the phone call. Finds the funding. Keeps you on schedule. Clears the way and solves all the problems it can until the human part, the wanting and the dreaming, is all that’s left. 
Here’s the best part: we have no idea what people will want. The world until now has been shaped by the small number of fanatics who have somehow found a way to make their wants real. But we’ve never seen humanity with every single person’s agency fully switched on. Eight billion people who just need to write their dream down in order to get started making it happen.
So we built Muse to help people build the world they want.
Here’s to wanting. Here’s to dreaming. Here’s to everyone.

full_text:
the most underrated part of muse is the model that powers it. thank you to the MSL research team—some of the most technically brilliant, hardworking scientists and engineers i’ve ever known. you brought original ideas to difficult problems, invented new methods, and battled through enormous technical complexity to build the jewel at the heart of muse.

thank you to the teams working on agentic post-training, tool and computer use, memory, personalization, alignment, safety, and multimodal understanding. thank you to the people building data, evals, and infrastructure beneath it all. so much scientific ingenuity lives in those details: designing a better experiment, finding the flaw in an apparently good result, staying with a stubborn problem until a new way forward becomes clear.

and now that jewel powers a beautiful product your grandma can use without knowing a thing about the extraordinary complexity underneath. it will just work for her. all those discoveries, all that patient work, becoming something simple and useful in another person’s hands. there is something magical about that. i’m grateful to be building with you.

full_text:
We believe strongly in the necessity to invest into alignment.

1. People and businesses will only use agents that are aligned with their intent and values. If we do not build models aligned with people and businesses, then they will move to more aligned options.

2. Every lab should have a strong governance framework across training and deployment. This should include external evaluators, which are best practice for transparency, and independent oversight on things like safety criteria for model launches.

3. Every lab will need to operate within institutional protections of democratic countries. This means labs face significant liability if their models cause harm. This will push the ecosystem in the right ways.

4. Advances in the field are ultimately downstream of compute and resource allocation. Racing on recursive self-improvement is one of the riskiest pathways for potential loss of control to powerful models. Meta is committing the significant majority of our compute towards serving people rather than racing on RSI, and other labs can choose to do the same.

AI is a very powerful technology, and there is immense responsibility in developing it safely alongside the right checks and balances.

full_text:
something people may have missed:

we have been building our models (muse spark 1 through 1.3) specifically to be exceptional for muse over many months.

in each of our releases, we made big gains on agentic and multimodal capability. each of these steps were secretly to set the stage for our personal agent, @Muse. (they’re named the same thing for a reason… we planned ahead!)

when we started MSL last year, the goal was always to develop personal superintelligence. that always meant giving AI superpowers to everyone in the world, and the personal agent is the perfect manifestation of that.

building great models takes time, and it takes an enormous amount of planning and foresight to develop unique capabilities into these models. it often requires months of careful research and work across infra and data to build excellent models.

it is very sweet to see the culmination of over a year of hard work come together into a product that people are loving. we are so glad that people are enjoying muse, and we can’t wait to keep improving it!

fun fact: the muse feed was my idea (one of the few things that was) after realizing agents with strong memory recommend content to you in a very different way than existing recommendation systems

they’re much closer to a good friend sending you things they think you might like based on what they knows about you, vs a slew of content related to what you just clicked.

it’s just the beginning here, but very excited for people to try their muse feeds and see what they do with it!

full_text:
What does DeepSeek R1 & v3 mean for LLM data?

Contrary to some lazy takes I’ve seen, DeepSeek R1 was trained on a shit ton of human-generated data—in fact, the DeepSeek models are setting records for the disclosed amount of post-training data for open-source models:

- 600,000 reasoning data [1]
- 200,000 non-reasoning SFT data [2]
- human preference (RLHF) dataset of undisclosed size [3]
- human-processed synthetic data for cold-start data [4]

According to Chinese AI engineers, DeepSeek actually values data annotation even more than other Chinese labs, with the CEO personally labeling data for the model [5] (This reminds me of @karpathy who used to spend a quarter of his time labeling at Tesla). The DeepSeek-v3 paper even has a dedicated acknowledgement section for Data Annotation [6].
DeepSeek-V3, which was distilled from DeepSeek-R1, was also trained on an instruction-tuning dataset of 1.5M samples. [7]

These SFT datasets are even larger than other open-source models:

- Qwen-2.5 was trained on 1M SFT samples [8]
- the last time Meta disclosed was for Llama 2, which was trained on only 30k SFT samples and 3M RLHF samples [9]
- Kimi k1.5 was trained on roughly 1M SFT, 1M multi-modal SFT, 800k samples for classic reward modeling, and another 800k CoT labeled examples for reasoning [10] 

It’s interesting that the size of the RLHF dataset was undisclosed, while they disclosed the size of the SFT and reasoning datasets. This could be because it is much larger than one would expect, or it reveals some interesting technical detail they don’t care to share. Human preference datasets are often much larger than SFT datasets in most models, so a reasonable estimate would be that DeepSeek’s models are probably trained on at least 3-5M samples, which is quite a large preference dataset!

The main technical breakthrough of DeepSeek-R1 is that for reasoning, you can forgo SFT data in favor of reasoning data—but reasoning data is still human data of difficult problems&answers in a variety of domains. 

The reasoning dataset is actually quite large—600k reasoning samples is a LOT. This is in line with a broader trend we’ve seen from SFT data towards other data types like human preference/RLHF data and reasoning data. This is for technical reasons—SFT caps the performance of the model at a certain level, whereas RLHF or other methods enable the models to continue improving without bound beyond the limits of the dataset.

DeepSeek R1 is a very exciting model, and it’s great to see o1 reasoning capabilities replicated in the wild. In terms of training data, however, the DeepSeek models are actually setting open-source records in terms of the amount of human data used.

DeepSeek-V3, which was distilled from DeepSeek-R1, was also trained on an instruction-tuning dataset of 1.5M samples. [7]

These SFT datasets are even larger than other open-source models:

- Qwen-2.5 was trained on 1M SFT samples [8]
- the last time Meta disclosed was for Llama 2, which was trained on only 30k SFT samples and 3M RLHF samples [9]
- Kimi k1.5 was trained on roughly 1M SFT, 1M multi-modal SFT, 800k samples for classic reward modeling, and another 800k CoT labeled examples for reasoning [10] 

It’s interesting that the size of the RLHF dataset was undisclosed, while they disclosed the size of the SFT and reasoning datasets. This could be because it is much larger than one would expect, or it reveals some interesting technical detail they don’t care to share. Human preference datasets are often much larger than SFT datasets in most models, so a reasonable estimate would be that DeepSeek’s models are probably trained on at least 3-5M samples, which is quite a large preference dataset!

The main technical breakthrough of DeepSeek-R1 is that for reasoning, you can forgo SFT data in favor of reasoning data—but reasoning data is still human data of difficult problems&answers in a variety of domains. 

The reasoning dataset is actually quite large—600k reasoning samples is a LOT. This is in line with a broader trend we’ve seen from SFT data towards other data types like human preference/RLHF data and reasoning data. This is for technical reasons—SFT caps the performance of the model at a certain level, whereas RLHF or other methods enable the models to continue improving without bound beyond the limits of the dataset.

DeepSeek R1 is a very exciting model, and it’s great to see o1 reasoning capabilities replicated in the wild. In terms of training data, however, the DeepSeek models are actually setting open-source records in terms of the amount of human data used.

At the YC Alumni Reunion, I got lots of questions from new founders about how to build a successful company, but realized that they all had the same answer. And it’s this:

—————————————————

DO TOO MUCH

As a new founder, I’d often look at the CEOs of successful companies and wonder, “How do they do it?”

As Scale grows and as I learn on the job, I’ve come to realize that leaders of great organizations never just do it. They overdo it.

As a leader, you are the upper bound for how much anyone in your company will care. You need to do more, care more, attempt more than would seem reasonable. It will seem like overkill. But too much is the right amount.

This is true in big and small ways.

- What people say is overoptimism is just optimism.
- What people say is overcommunicating is just communicating.
- What people say is overdelivering is just delivering.
- What people say is micromanagement is just management.
- What people say is ruthless prioritization is just prioritization.

Actually living this way will seem crazy, and that’s ok. There is no Apple without Jobs’s “obsessive” attention to detail. There is no SpaceX or Tesla without Elon’s “maniacal” drive for execution. I have never seen ordinary effort lead to extraordinary results.

If we had not done too much, Scale would not be the company it is today.

When AI really started to take off in 2022 and “generative AI” became a thing, within 6 months Scale shifted the vast majority of our team to working on generating data for scaling LLMs.

Most companies would go through quarters of bureaucratic planning cycles and only move after a competitor started eating their lunch. In our case, the change was drastic and abrupt — some might say jarring or extreme.

What people might have reasonably described as overreacting was just reacting. And in hindsight, that reaction to developments in AI was what made Scale’s subsequent path possible, including growing 4X over the last year.

What we’ve accomplished to date represents the compounded results of everybody embracing the culture of overdoing. Scale will do things incumbent companies wouldn’t, because it’s simply too scary or painful, but others not going to the same lengths is a feature not a bug.

Creating something meaningful is a beautiful, and yes, scary and painful thing. And if you’re not overdoing it, you’re underdoing it.
